Daniel’s “abstraction boundary” framing is strongest when it treats the player’s understanding as a *stack of models*—but it also smuggles in a hidden assumption: that the “right” abstraction is the one the game has been “training.” In circuits, a boundary is often enforced by physics (noise, coupling, tolerances) whether you like it or not; in games, the “analog layer” (the physics engine, update loop, collision rules) is itself authored. So the Anti-Chamber door puzzle isn’t merely a boundary *breaking* so much as a boundary *re-ranking*: the game reveals that “doors are conditionals” was a convenience abstraction, not a guaranteed contract. That difference matters because it’s basically a question of design fairness—what cues did the game provide about which abstractions are safe to rely on, and when it’s legitimate to demand the player reason at a lower level?

There’s a useful connection here to classic game-studies language about the [magic circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_circle_(virtual_worlds)) (Huizinga): some puzzles “break” boundaries by forcing attention to layers the player thought were outside the circle (UI, save files, controller inputs), while others do it by forcing attention *downward* into the simulation’s materiality (timing, inertia, spatial occlusion). Anti-Chamber’s example is mostly the latter: it asks the player to stop treating a door as a boolean gate and instead treat it as a moving body with momentum and time—closer to “engineering reasoning” than “logic reasoning.” That’s not necessarily unfit; it’s a shift in what counts as the game’s stable ontology. The critique to press is whether the game signposted that ontology shift, or simply rewarded players who already suspected the engine could be exploited.

If Daniel wants other clear cases, they tend to cluster into two families. **“Rule-layer literalization”**: *Baba Is You* turns the abstraction itself into manipulable objects (“DOOR IS SHUT”), collapsing boundary and rulebook into one surface. **“Meta-layer intrusion”**: games like *Pony Island* and *Inscryption* (and earlier, *Metal Gear Solid*’s Psycho Mantis gimmick) force the player to treat menus, resets, files, or peripherals as part of the puzzle, which is a different kind of boundary violation than physics-based timing. And then there are **“knowledge gates”** like *Outer Wilds*, where progression depends on reinterpreting what you thought the world’s rules were—less about twitch execution, more about realizing your prior abstraction was incomplete. These examples suggest a refinement to Daniel’s question: is the pleasure coming from breaking an abstraction boundary, or from discovering which boundaries were *never promised* in the first place?
